name: Sunbed + MT2 stack

lead: The stack combines melanotan II, an unlicensed tanning peptide, with tanning bed sessions to darken skin faster and deeper. It circulates in looksmaxxing tanning discussions, with users reporting a deep tan in fewer sessions.

The chain is two-part: melanotan II mimics alpha-MSH to stimulate melanin production, while UV light triggers tanning directly, and proponents expect the two to add together. Each part is known to darken skin on its own; no studies have tested the combination.

paras: Users combine the peptide with regular sunbed sessions over several weeks, in the belief that melanin is already primed when UV arrives. Descriptions come from user reports rather than trials.

Melanotan II is unlicensed and regulators have warned against it since 2007. UV tanning devices are classified by IARC as Group 1 carcinogens and are linked to higher melanoma risk; reviews note melanoma reports in melanotan users may reflect extra UV exposure.

angle.text: You combine tanning-bed sessions with melanotan II to build a deep tan in fewer sessions than either alone: the peptide boosts melanin production and UV triggers pigment. Each part is known to darken skin by itself. The combination has not been trialled and rests on user reports.

lead: The sunbed plus MT2 stack is a looksmaxxing practice that pairs indoor tanning sessions with melanotan II (MT2), an unlicensed synthetic analogue of the hormone alpha-MSH, to build a deep tan faster than either would alone. Users want darker, more even skin colour, which many in these communities say adds contrast, definition and a healthier, more attractive look.[1][2][3]

Melanotan II stimulates melanin production, and its reversible effects include darkening of moles and freckles, flushing, nausea and, in men, erections. It has never been approved as a medicine, and unlicensed products are sold online and in some gyms and salons.[1] Indoor tanning devices emit mostly UVA with a little UVB; improving appearance is the most commonly cited reason people tan indoors.[2]

Health agencies have warned against unlicensed melanotan since 2007, and the World Health Organization classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen. Wikipedia notes that reported melanomas in melanotan users coincided with heavy sunbathing and sunbed use, and that a 2021 review said higher melanoma rates among users probably reflect greater UV exposure.[1][2] No clinical trial of the combination has been published.
infobox: Health agencies since 2007 (MT2); WHO Group 1 carcinogen (UV)[1][2]

paras: The stack is the combination of two separate practices. Melanotan II acts on melanocortin receptors to increase melanin and may increase sexual arousal through MC4 receptor activation.[1] Sunbeds darken existing melanin with UVA and, through their small UVB output, stimulate new melanin.[2] Users describe the pairing as a way to need fewer or shorter sunbed sessions, a belief that rests on community reports rather than trials.[3]

Scientists at the University of Arizona developed melanotan I and II in the 1980s as possible sunless tanning agents. Melanotan I (afamelanotide) was licensed to an Australian start-up that became Clinuvel, and the FDA approved afamelanotide in 2019 for a rare genetic sun sensitivity. Melanotan II was licensed for sexual dysfunction research but never approved; Palatin stopped development in 2000 and moved to bremelanotide, approved by the FDA in 2019.[1]

Agencies in Norway (December 2007), Denmark (2008), the UK (2008), Ireland (February 2009) and the FDA (a warning letter in January 2009) issued warnings about unlicensed products, citing legality, case reports and possible impurities.[1]

Friedrich Wolff invented the sunbed in 1975, and salons spread across Europe and North America in the late 1970s.[2] High-pressure beds can deliver 10 to 15 times the UVA of midday sun.[2] A 2022 review described sunbed exposure as having well-documented harms and no clear benefit beyond cosmetic outcomes.[4]

Wikipedia reports a relative melanoma risk of 1.20 for ever-users and 1.59 for those who began before age 35 (2012 analysis), and notes links to skin ageing, burns and eye damage.[2] A BMJ meta-analysis estimated the melanoma burden attributable to sunbed use in western Europe.[5] Regulation includes Brazil's 2009 ban on cosmetic use and Australia's 2015 ban on commercial tanning.[2]

No studies found on the combination. Studies of sunbeds alone are observational and meta-analytic, for example a 2012 BMJ systematic review of melanoma attributable to sunbed use and a 2019 review on sunbeds and melanoma risk.[5][6] For melanotan II, Wikipedia cites a 2013 review finding no conclusive evidence it causes melanoma, a 2021 review attributing higher melanoma risk among users to greater UV exposure, and a 2020 in vivo study in which it suppressed melanoma progression.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sunbed use is debated as a way to improve looks, with posters weighing short-term appearance against cancer risk.[3][7][8]
